procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of the learned Division Bench of Madras High Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The text mentions Exhibit P1 judgment, and the petitioners sought to call for records leading to Exhibits P3, P7, and P9, and to set aside Exhibits P3, P7, and P9 via a writ of certiorari.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court admitted Special Leave Petitions as Civil Appeal Nos. 7208-7209 of 2005. Additionally, the Supreme Court transferred T.P. (C) No. 2849 of 2019 to Transferred Case (Civil) No. 29 of 2021. The Supreme Court also heard Writ Petitions and Transferred Cases, consolidating many cases into one hearing.

directions: The writ petitions as well as all the transferred cases are disposed of in the aforesaid terms.

issue.issue_text: Whether the restrictions imposed are arbitrary and illegal and therefore, impermissible under Article 14 of the Constitution?

law: A challenge to the validity of rules under Article 14 of the Constitution can be assessed based on whether there is a valid classification.
application: The Court analyzed the challenge to the rules on the ground of arbitrariness under Article 14.
It found that the rules were based on a valid classification.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the restrictions were arbitrary and illegal under Article 14, holding that the challenge must fail because the rules were based on a valid classification.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the restrictions imposed are arbitrary and illegal and therefore, impermissible under Article 14 of the Constitution?
appellant_arguments: The petitioners challenged the validity of Chapter VI of the Council Guidelines No.1-CA(7)/02/2008 issued by the respondent-Institute.
respondent_arguments: The writ petitions and transferred cases challenging the validity of the guidelines are devoid of any merit and should be dismissed.

statutes.section: The Act as a whole, with specific reference to Sections 2, 15, 30B, and the Second Schedule.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A person should not be penalised except under clear law. This principle forms part of the context against which legislation is enacted and, when interpreting legislation, a court should take it into account.
obiter: There is uncertainty in the law when a guideline is successfully assailed in a High Court, an interim stay is granted on that judgment by the Supreme Court, and the matter remains pending.
A stay on the operation of a judgment is not a declaration that the judgment was bad in law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that the ability for Chartered Accountants to conduct compulsory tax audits under Section 44AB of the IT Act is not a fundamental right inherent to their profession, but rather a privilege extended to them in the public interest. Because this function is a privilege, the respondent-Institute, as an expert body, has the authority to impose reasonable restrictions, such as a cap on the number of audits, to regulate that privilege and ensure the quality of audits for the benefit of the public exchequer. Such a restriction, having a rational nexus to its objective, is not arbitrary or unreasonable.
legal_tests_applied: The test for a reasonable restriction under Article 19(6) requires adjudging it not against theoretical standards, but in light of the nature of the right, the interest of the general public sought to be secured, and the reasonableness of the quality and extent of the fetter upon the right.

The reasonableness of a restriction is to be determined in an objective manner from the standpoint of the interests of the general public, not the interests of the persons upon whom the restrictions are imposed. The court must consider the nature of the right, the underlying purpose of the restriction, the extent and urgency of the evil sought to be remedied, the disproportion of the imposition, and the prevailing conditions.
A just balance must be struck between the fundamental rights of the individual and the larger and broader interest of society.
Restrictions imposed that appear to be consistent with the Directive Principles of State Policy in Part IV of the Constitution are to be upheld as being in the public interest and reasonable.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioners' reliance on the case of Institute of Chartered Financial Analysts of India was misplaced, as that case dealt with the acquisition of an additional qualification, which was not found to be against the public interest, whereas the current restriction is intended to protect the quality of a statutory responsibility.

The argument that the restriction is unreasonable because it causes hardship to a certain section of professionals was rejected, as a restriction cannot be deemed unreasonable merely because it operates harshly in a given case.

The court rejected the foundational premise that conducting tax audits was a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g). Instead, it was framed as a privilege, which can be reasonably regulated: "Compulsory tax audits was neither an inherent part of the practice of Chartered Accountant nor essential function which could be claimed as a fundamental right u/Art.19(1)(g)."
why_respondent_won: The restriction was found to be in the public interest, specifically to ensure the quality of tax audit reports for the benefit of the public exchequer. The court must consider the public interest from the perspective of the general public, not just the Chartered Accountants.

The court accepted that since public interest was the genesis of the privilege being extended to Chartered Accountants, it is reasonable for the respondent-Institute, as an expert body, to regulate that privilege to serve the public interest.

The restriction was supported by external evidence of its necessity, particularly the CAG’s recommendation to the Government to insert a statutory provision capping the number of tax audits to ensure quality.

The restriction was analogous to an existing, accepted regulation under Section 224 of the Companies Act, which also limits the number of audits a firm can conduct, demonstrating a parliamentary intent to regulate the profession to maintain standards and quality.
The court found that the restriction has a rational nexus with the objects sought to be achieved, and where such a nexus exists, the restriction cannot be held unreasonable.
policy_considerations: In a welfare State, a fine balance must be maintained between the public interest of the community and the liberties of the individual.
Individual rights must be delicately balanced with the constitutional imperative of the 'ordered progress of society towards a welfare state.'

The court should defer to the Legislature or an expert body in appreciating the needs of the people and should only interfere when a statute or guideline is clearly violative of a constitutional right.
Restrictions that are in furtherance of the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV of the Constitution) should be upheld as being in the public interest and reasonable.
